episode_title: Ep. #44, Beyond the Model: Observing AI Agents with Mikyo King
question: How does Arize use OpenTelemetry for AI agent observability?
transcript_excerpt: All solutions around agent observability at Arize revolve around open telemetry. OpenTelemetry comes from traditionally the DevOps world, and while it comes with some overhead, it is the most common ground through which agents are able to observe data. Teams are already onboarded to OTEL, making it a huge unlock for agents because there are many unknown unknowns in agents on top of DevOps. OTEL has been a really good medium and the right way of thinking of things as they scale up.

episode_title: Ep. #44, Beyond the Model: Observing AI Agents with Mikyo King
question: What is the difference between Open Telemetry semantics and OpenInference semantics for AI observability?
transcript_excerpt: OpenTelemetry is a general idea that applications have three primary signals: tracing (hierarchical interactions composed of spans that chain across network boundaries), structured logging, and metrics through Prometheus. With agents, you need to understand how they behave from the outside because code no longer just documents agent behavior—you don't know how many times it will loop or if it goes into code mode. OpenTelemetry specifically tracing can give understanding of that system from the outside, while semantics codify what that means (for example, db.xyz means something specific). Arize has been building those semantics over three years for agent-specific conventions.

episode_title: Ep. #44, Beyond the Model: Observing AI Agents with Mikyo King
question: How should teams approach starting with evaluations for AI agents?
transcript_excerpt: You don't have to start with evals—it depends on how critical what you're building is. Evaluations work like layers of Swiss cheese with different layers and levels, and none of them will be perfect, but you want to guarantee that as the frontier shifts or model decisions change your system continues working. Evaluations can be a way to sift through data and don't always have to be perfect signals; people will use your platform in ways you didn't anticipate, so you can use LLM power to classify intent, segment data by region, or detect changing language patterns.

episode_title: Ep. #44, Beyond the Model: Observing AI Agents with Mikyo King
question: Why did Arize choose to open source AI observability tooling instead of building a closed SaaS product?
transcript_excerpt: The decision to open source predates the LLM boom. At the time, if you were building AI or LLMs, every developer's tech stack was open source using tools like Keras and MLflow. If you had a SaaS platform, it had to be exponentially better than open source to even be considered. Beyond developer adoption, there's a mission-driven approach: everyone is learning about building AI and LLMs, and you trust the vendor that open sources everything where you can read the code. Additionally, in this new market, open sourcing shapes the industry and vertical by defining what evals and telemetry mean, and it enables collaboration and community contributions.

episode_title: Ep. #44, Beyond the Model: Observing AI Agents with Mikyo King
question: What security challenges does Arize face when open sourcing AI agent observability?
transcript_excerpt: Cybersecurity is a particularly tough challenge. With closed source projects, it's harder to identify multi-vector attacks, but with open source it's much more likely attackers can figure out those attacks. The biggest current crack is that foundation model providers route cyber offensive capabilities to fallback models, making it impossible for even financially-backed open source projects to use frontier-class models' cyber expertise. This forces consideration of open-weight models for cyber defensive capabilities because attackers' capabilities are extremely emergent right now.

episode_title: Ep. #44, Beyond the Model: Observing AI Agents with Mikyo King
question: How should open source maintainers handle pull requests from AI coding agents?
transcript_excerpt: Pull requests used to be valuable for their code, but now the idea is what matters most. If a pull request has a good idea, maintainers should have agency to close it while saying the contribution will inform roadmap decisions even if the code isn't taken as-is. The challenge is distinguishing genuine human pain points—where someone spent time trying things and showing their work—from agent-generated contributions that can be overzealous. For product decisions and storytelling, maintainers need to retain strong opinions and agency because informed decisions like making telemetry immutable for banking auditability require domain-specific knowledge.
